paragraphs: Hattora lo asera ella yen nesek shennitnassek laaboda zara (debarim lb, lch), vaasarattu bishtiyya ubahanaa deittaqqash lezibche aboda zara (aboda zara kt, b). ak rabbotenu za"l aseru apillu setam yenam shel goyim vegam aseru maggaan beyayin shellanu - hen bishtiyya hen bahanaa - kedin yen nesek, velo chillequ bo kelum. v"p sheameru hattaam shel haggezera hazzot hu bishbil benotehem shello yabou lehityached immahem veyabou al yede kak lide zenut velide chittun - en zeh hu iqqar hattaam ella hemma rau berucha qadesham taam sod nistar venelam beissur zeh vegazeru alayv. vederek hachakamim shello legallot taam hassodi veraq omerim taam happeshati. lekak apillu im mitbattel taam happeshati beezeh zeman - lo yitbattel taam hassodi ad olam.

clarification.explanation: By Torah law, only "libation wine" is forbidden — wine actually poured out for idolatry — and its prohibition covers both drinking and benefit, since it was equated to idolatrous sacrifices. But the Sages broadened the prohibition, forbidding also gentiles' "ordinary wine" (their regular wine, even if not actually dedicated to idolatry) and its contact with our wine — both for drinking and benefit, making no distinction between the cases. Although a simple reason was given for this decree (concern that through wine one might grow close to gentile women, leading to promiscuity or intermarriage), this is not the only true reason — the Sages perceived, through their holy spirit, a secret and hidden reason for this prohibition, but their way was not to reveal the secret reason, only the simple one. Therefore, even if the simple reason should cease to apply at some point (for example, if there is no concern of intermarriage), the prohibition never ceases, since it rests on the eternal, secret reason.
takeaways: Torah law forbids only wine actually poured for idolatry; the Sages broadened this to forbid gentiles' ordinary wine and its contact with our wine, for both drinking and benefit.
The stated reason (concern of intermarriage) is not the only true reason — there is a hidden, secret reason, so the prohibition never lapses even if the stated reason no longer applies.

paragraphs: Al ken issur zeh en lo hetter leolam beshum zeman ubeshum maqom veonesh haober al zeh gadol meod ki oqer nishmato mimmaqom shennishresha veen lo cheleq laolam habba. ukemo shekkatub bazzohar haqqadosh parashat shemini (ch"g m, ). venitchabber al issur zeh seper meyuchad hanniqra "yayin hamshummar" vehaqqore bo tesammer saarat besaro miggodel haonesh. veayyen beseper "ayumma kenigdalot" dap k"d maaseh nora min hammikshol sheyyatza mishshetiyyat setam yenam leechad asar chakamim, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: This prohibition (ordinary gentile wine and its contact) has no leniency ever, at any time or place, and the penalty for transgressing it is extremely severe, since it uproots one's soul from its root and forfeits one's share in the World to Come — as explained in the holy Zohar. A special book called "Yayin HaMeshumar" was composed on this, whose reading arouses great fear at the severity of the penalty, and it relates a terrible incident of a mishap that befell eleven Sages as a result of drinking ordinary gentile wine.
takeaways: The prohibition of ordinary gentile wine and its contact never lapses — the penalty is especially severe (forfeiting one's share in the World to Come), as explained in the Zohar.

paragraphs: Mihu lo aseru chaza"l setam yenam umaggaan beyayin shellanu gam bahanaa ella raq baggoyim obede aboda zara, abal goyim sheen obedim aboda zara kegon yishmeelim sheen lahem pesilim vaaboda zara - en setam yenam umaggaan beyayin shellanu asur bahanaa ella raq asur bishtiyya bilbad. velaken im goy yishmael naga beyayin shellanu eno osero bahanaa ella raq bishtiyya mippene shehayyishmeelim modim beyichud veen lahem pesel velo mine aboda zara kelal. veken meporash bitshubat haramba"m teshuba q"s dap l"d ammud g' bitshubot veaggadot hannidpas belipesa ayyen sham. veken mukach middibre rabbenu haari"y za"l beshaar taame hammitzot yeuyyan sham. veayyen peri toar yoreh dea siman d' seip qatan y" yeuyyan sham. umah shekkatab harab birke yosep za"l al dibre peri toar hannizkar - kebar chazar bo besipro marit haayin dap "t ", vesham tziyyen al teshubat haramba"m za"l shezzakarti leel.

Veotam haggoyim sheddarkam lissa sheti vaereb bebigdehem veyesh lahem gam ken sheti vaereb bebet tepillatam shemmishtachavim lo - az setam yenam umaggaan beyayin shellanu asur gam bahanaa, ki ellu en lahem yichud hashshem karauy veyesh lahem shittup. vehayyichud sheosim hu yichud sheyyesh bo dopi kayyadua. veayyen bene yaaqob sheela g' dap qp"t:

clarification.explanation: The Sages forbade ordinary gentile wine and its contact for benefit only regarding idol-worshiping gentiles, but gentiles who do not worship idols — such as Ishmaelites (Muslims), who have no idols or idolatry — their ordinary wine and its contact with our wine is not forbidden for benefit, only for drinking. Therefore if an Ishmaelite touched our wine, this forbids it only for drinking, not for benefit, since Ishmaelites believe in God's unity and have no idolatry at all — as the Rambam wrote in his responsa, and as implied by the Arizal's words. But regarding gentiles who have a cross (crosswise) on their garments and in their house of worship, which they bow to — their ordinary wine and its contact is forbidden even for benefit, since their faith is not pure unity but "association" (unity with a flaw).
takeaways: Contact by a Muslim gentile (an Ishmaelite, who believes in God's unity) forbids wine only for drinking, not for benefit.
Contact by a Christian-associationist gentile (with a cross) forbids it even for benefit.

paragraphs: "p sheamarnu goy obed aboda zara oser hayyayin gam bahanaa mikkol maqom im hu tinoq sheeno makkir sheeno makkir haaboda zara umeshammesheha eno oser hayyayin bemaggao bahanaa ella raq asur bishtiyya vaapillu im hu tinoq ben yomo oser bishtiyya mihu tinoq yishmeeli im hu qatan sheen lo kavvanat magga eno oser hayyayin shellanu bemagga apillu bishtiyya dekevan shehu miyyishmeelim sheen lahem aboda zara vehu odennu tinoq sheen lo kavvanat magga eno oser kelal veayyen qehal yeuddeh za"l besiman qk"d ot ':

clarification.explanation: Although an idol-worshiping gentile forbids wine even for benefit, this is not true of an infant who does not yet understand what idolatry is — his contact forbids only for drinking, not for benefit, even if he is a newborn infant (very new). But a small Ishmaelite infant, who has no intent or awareness of contact at all — his contact does not forbid the wine even for drinking, since he is anyway from a people with no idolatry, and additionally is an infant with no intent of contact.
takeaways: An idol-worshiping gentile's infant who touched wine forbids it only for drinking, not for benefit.
A small Ishmaelite infant with no intent does not forbid it at all.

paragraphs: Sapeq setam yenam umaggaan shel yishmeelim muttar apillu bishtiyya velaken debash hannaaseh mittirosh hambushshal shel anabim shemmokerim yisrael veyesh chashash shemmeorab bo tirosh shel goyim yishmeelim shebbeoto hammaqom hare zeh muttar veken heid rabbenu morenu harab chayyim veyittol za"l al rabbenu haggadol vehechasid rabbenu haari"y zlh"h shehaya okel mizzeh shehu besapeq veeno choshesh vekannizkar beshaar taame hammitzot parashat eqeb:

clarification.explanation: In a case of doubt whether an Ishmaelite touched the wine, it is permitted to drink it, since even certain Ishmaelite contact does not forbid for benefit (only for drinking, and here it is only a doubt). Therefore, honey made from cooked grape must sold by Jews, with concern it may have mixed with Ishmaelites' grape must from the same region, is permitted. And so Rabbi Chaim Vital testified regarding his teacher the Arizal, that he would eat such a thing, which was only a doubt, without concern.
takeaways: Doubt of Ishmaelite contact with wine is permitted even for drinking, and therefore products with a remote concern of mixing with Ishmaelite grape must are permitted.

paragraphs: Ledidan bene hasseparaddim sheqqibbalnu alenu horaat maran za"l haddin hu ben setam yayin shel haakku"m uben hammagga shellahem beyayin shellanu asur bahanaa legamre veen lemakero legoy o litteno bemattana ella yishpekennu bachapira shebbaqqarqa beopen shello yehaneh mimmennu veen lehaqel bazeh gam bazeh hazzeman veayyen bene yaaqob dap qp"t v"chiqre leb" yoreh dea siman qtz"t dap r"t yeuyyan sham vehinneh ledaat ha"keneset haggedola" behaggahat habbet yosep ot y' man deasar setam yenam bahanaa gam bazzeman hazzeh, hu haddin name deoser gam ken leqabbel setam yenam min haggoy bechobo ulepi daat gam maran za"l deu ken mihu harab "torat chesed" siman y"ch sebira lah degam haoserim setam yenam bahanaa bazzeman hazzeh mattirim ligbot setam yenam bechobo mishshum dehave kematztzil miyyadam yeuyyan sham ak hareayot shehebi lazeh enam mukrachot deyesh lidchot kaasher yireh haroeh amenam harab zekor leabraham cheleq ' dap rl"d ammud b' hebi mipposeq echad sheheela lehattir liqqach setam yenam bishbil chobo im en beyado ligbot mishshear nekasim mitteshubat harashba" za"l veyadua ki harashba" za"l hu min hassoberim deasur setam yenam bahanaa gam bazzeman hazzeh ulepi daat harab hannizkar gam maran za"l dato haki veal ken yesh lehorot demuttar leqabbel setam yenam bechobo im en dabar acher leqabbel mehem abal vadday deasur laasot sechora bistam yenam vezeh pashut:

clarification.explanation: The Sephardim, who accepted Maran's (the Shulchan Aruch's) ruling upon themselves, are accustomed to be stringent: both idol-worshipers' ordinary wine and their contact with our wine are entirely forbidden for benefit, even in our time — and it may not be sold to a gentile or given as a gift, but must be poured into a pit in the ground so that no one benefits from it. The ruling also addresses a case where a gentile owes a Jew money and wishes to repay the debt with wine — there is a dispute among the authorities whether it is permitted to accept the wine as debt payment (like "rescuing from their hands"), but the conclusion is that it is permitted to accept ordinary gentile wine as debt payment if there is no other way to collect, but it is absolutely forbidden to trade in it (to buy and sell it as a business).
takeaways: For Sephardim, ordinary gentile wine and its contact are entirely forbidden for benefit, even today — it must be poured out with no benefit, not sold or given as a gift.
It is permitted to accept ordinary gentile wine as debt payment if there is no other option, but absolutely forbidden to trade in it.

paragraphs: Shekar sheosin min hayyayin sheqqorin oto berendi asur lishtoto ki kevan shehaya yayin gamur battechilla beyad haobed kokabim umazzalot (akku"m) shub en lo hetter beshannoto et tamo veosehu shekar "y bishshul mechadash deha kebar neesar beodo yayin veayyen lehaggaon chida" za"l besipro marit haayin dap "v al gab shennishal al moreh shura al shekar niqra "anvavh ardeyineti" (berendi italqi meanabim) shel akku"m letzarepo od tzerup echad umuttar bishtiyya al pi teshuba shehubea beseper admat qodesh cheleq b' siman y"g veheshib haggaon chida" za"l dezeh hashshekar hu gupo shel issur mammash shehu kocho verucho shel hayyayin veim od yetzarepennu tzerup achar tzerup hu haissur atzmo umishshibcho yoter velo paqa issureh yeuyyan sham:

Veda deap al gab deyimmatze beare eroppa batte charoshet sheosim mizzeh hashshekar shel hayyayin bekashrut "y yisrael mittechilla vead sop behashgachat harab shel oto maqom veod gam ken yadanu ki nitchaddesh bazeh hazzeman beir haqqodesh yapo tvb"b sheosin mizzeh hashshekar shel hayyayin al yede yisrael bishbil sechora vesholechim mimmennu harbeh limkor beare eroppa im kol zeh shekar zeh shemmebiim socharim goyim limqomotenu limkor asur bishtiyya deqayma lan kol deparesh merubba paresh veharob hu yayin haasur mihu nireh deyesh lehattiro bahanaa gam ledidan vegam yesh lehattir lahabio hayisrael meare eroppa lehistacher bimqomot ellu deikka bazeh telat sepeqe vehu sapeq shemma zeh hashshekar shebba lo mehatam hu naasa "y yisrael bekashrut hen beotam meqomot hen meitto shel ir haqqodesh yapo tvb"b sheshsholechim lesham veim timtze lomar zeh naasa bebet charoshet shel goyim shemma happoalim sheasequ bazeh hem hayu kullam meotam sheenam modim bedat acher veen lahem sheti vaereb veen modim bo deillu min haddin en oserim hayyayin bahanaa ella raq bishtiyya kedin hayyishmeelim veim timtze lomar deellu happoalim sheasequ bazeh hashshekar hem akku"m shemma halaka keman desabar bazzeman hazzeh en haakku"m oserim setam yenam bahanaa v"g desapeq zeh hu keneged sebarat maran za"l kebar heelinu bemaqom acher denukal laasot sepeq sepeqa sheyyesh bo tzad echad shehu neged maran za"l sheqqibbalnu horaotayv laken gam ledidan nukal lehattir laasot beshekar zeh sechora veraq bishtiyya asur:

clarification.explanation: Brandy made from wine is forbidden to drink, since once it was actual wine in a gentile's hand (and forbidden), it has no leniency even after its taste was changed through boiling and turning it into liquor, since it was already forbidden while still wine. Although there are factories in European cities (and even in the city of Jaffa) producing such brandy from wine with full kashrut, by a Jew under supervision — regarding brandy that gentile merchants bring here for sale, it is forbidden to drink, since by the halachic rule "whatever separates from a majority is attributed to the majority" — and most of this brandy originates from forbidden wine. But there is room to permit it for benefit (and even for Jews to trade in it, bring and sell it), since there are three combined doubts here: perhaps it was nevertheless made with proper kashrut; and if not, perhaps the workers involved were gentiles who do not worship idols (in which case it is permitted for benefit under the law of Ishmaelites); and if they were idol-worshipers, perhaps the halacha follows the view that in our time even such gentile contact does not forbid for benefit. These three doubts combine to permit the brandy for benefit and trade, but for drinking — it is forbidden.
takeaways: Brandy originating from gentile wine is forbidden for drinking, even after boiling and flavor change, and even where kosher factories exist, since most market brandy originates from forbidden wine.
For benefit and trade, it may be permitted by force of three combined doubts.

paragraphs: Yayin shemmearebin bo debash o pilpelin o debarim acherim im nishtanna tamo mechammatan "p shello nishtanna shemo eno neesar bemagga goy abal im notenim bo dabar muat sheeno mishtanneh tamo mechammatan eno moil kelum veayyen "shiyyure beraka" ot ch':

clarification.explanation: Wine mixed with honey, pepper, or other spices — if its taste genuinely changed due to the addition, even if the name is still "wine" (the name unchanged), it is no longer forbidden by gentile contact (since it is no longer considered ordinary wine). But if too small a quantity was added, not changing the taste, this accomplishes nothing — the wine is still considered ordinary wine and is forbidden by gentile contact.
takeaways: Wine mixed with honey or spice that genuinely changes its taste is no longer forbidden by gentile contact; a small addition not changing the taste accomplishes nothing.

paragraphs: Yayin mebushshal eno neesar bemagga goy umeematay niqra yayin mebushshal mishshehirticha al gab haesh venitmaet mimmiddato "y hareticha laken im rotzeh lebashshel hayyayin kede lehinnatzel mimmagga goy tzarik lebashshelo bishshul rab ad shettamo mishtanneh mittaam yayin letaam debash ukemo shekkatab haggaon chida" za"l besipro kikkar laden dap qs"b veayyen "keneset haggedola" haggahat habbet yosep ot yad' veerek hashshulchan ot Adonai ushear acharone umihu en habbishshul matztzil ella beyayin shello naga bo haggoy adayin abal im naga bo qodem habbishshul en habbishshul moil lehattiro veim ereb yayin mebushshal heteb im yayin sheeno mebushshal apillu shehahirrub hu yayin mibbishshul hare zeh neesar bemagga goy veayyen "shiyyure beraka" ot d':

clarification.explanation: Cooked wine is not forbidden by gentile contact. Wine is considered "cooked" only from the moment it was boiled on fire and its quantity diminished as a result of the boiling. Therefore one who wishes to cook his wine to escape the prohibition of gentile contact must cook it thoroughly, until the taste actually changes from a wine taste to a honey-like taste. Cooking rescues only wine the gentile has not yet touched — if the gentile already touched it before cooking, the cooking does not help permit it. And even if well-cooked wine was mixed with uncooked wine, even if most of the mixture is cooked wine, the entire mixture is forbidden by gentile contact (since part of it is still ordinary wine).
takeaways: Thoroughly cooked wine (until a noticeable taste change) is not forbidden by gentile contact — but only if the gentile has not already touched it before cooking, and only if the entire quantity is cooked (a mixture with uncooked wine is entirely forbidden).

paragraphs: Meematay niqra yayin sheyyeaser bemagga goy mishshehitchil lemeshek, dehaynu sheyyipneh hachartzannim vehazzaggim lemaqom echad venishar hayyayin lebaddo tzalul omed bemaqom echad zeh niqra hamshaka sheaz im naga bo haggoy neesar hakkol abal kol od shello hibdil hayyayin min hachartzannim vehazzaggim la have hamshaka. veillu laqach haggoy beyado mehaggat yayin harbeh im chartzannim vezaggim eno neesar zeh shebbeyado umuttar lehachaziro laggat abal im mille haggoy mehaggat kos yayin vekivven lishloto mechartzannim vezaggim have hamshaka veneesar kol mah shebbaggat:

clarification.explanation: Wine is considered "wine" for the purpose of the gentile-contact prohibition ("hamshakhah" — the drawing-off) only from the moment the seeds and skins (grape remnants) are separated from the clear wine, and the wine remains alone in a separate place. Until then, as long as the wine has not separated from the seeds, this is not yet "hamshakhah." Therefore, if a gentile took by hand a large quantity of wine together with seeds and skins from the winepress, what is in his hand does not become forbidden, and it is permitted to return it to the press. But if the gentile filled a full cup of wine from the press with the intent to drink it without seeds and skins, this is already "hamshakhah" and forbids all the wine in the press.
takeaways: The prohibition of gentile contact with press-wine applies only from the moment of "hamshakhah" — separating the clear wine from the seeds; before that, gentile contact with wine still mixed with seeds does not forbid it.

paragraphs: Yayin tzimmuqim shehem anabim yebeshim sheqqorin bearbe "zbyb" sheshshorin otam bemayim bechabit veosin otam yayin hare zeh yayin gamur veyesh bo nissuk vaapillu me sheriyyat hatztzimmuqim chashib yayin veneesar bemagga goy veayyen bashsha"k seip qatan k"g v"keneset haggedola" haggahat hattur ot tv'. velaken poh irenu sheshshorin tzimmuqin bemayim chammin beereb shabbat kede leqaddesh beshabbat beme sheriyyat tzimmuqim ellu tzerikin lehizzaher bahem mimmagga goy sheim naga bahem oser otam vehinneh bedin hahamshaka machmir mhrlb"ch betzimmuqin. ak rabbim choleqim alayv ukemo shekkatab b"shiyyure beraka" ot b' beorek, yeuyyan sham vaanachnu qayma lan kisbarat maran za"l diplig al mhrlb"ch za"l bazeh velaken yen tzimmuqin sheosim beirenu bagdad sheshshorin hatztzimmuqin bemayim bechabit esrim yom o yoter ubekol yom mehappekin hatztzimmuqin bemayim heteb beyadam ad shennaasin yayin az kol zeman shello mashak hayyayin min hatztzomeqin im naga bo goy eno oser:

clarification.explanation: Raisin wine (dried grapes) soaked in water in a barrel and made into wine is considered actual wine in every respect, including the prohibition of libation, and even the soaking water of the raisins themselves is considered wine and forbidden by gentile contact. One must therefore be especially careful with raisin wine customarily prepared on the Sabbath eve for Kiddush, that a gentile not touch it. There is a stringent opinion (the Maharalbach) holding that the law of "hamshakhah" is more lenient for raisins (that is, it becomes forbidden even before full separation), but many disagree with him, and it is accepted to rule following Maran, who disagrees with the Maharalbach — and therefore with raisin wine customarily made in Baghdad (soaking in water in a barrel for twenty days or more, with daily turning), as long as the wine has not been finally separated from the raisins, gentile contact does not forbid it.
takeaways: Raisin-soaking water is considered actual wine and forbidden by gentile contact; but as long as the wine has not been finally separated from the raisins (following Maran's view, which we follow), gentile contact does not forbid it.

paragraphs: Magga haakku"m sheoser hayyayin bahanaa hu sheyyigga beyado o beraglo o bedabar acher shebbeyado bekavvana vishakshek apillu shikshuk meat o sheshshata min haqqanqan shebbo hayyayin o shehigbihha hakkeli im hayyayin shebbo veshikshek meat vehakkeli haya patucha hinneh bekol zeh osero bahanaa abal im naga bayyayin velo shikshek kelal hare zeh muttar bahanaa veraq hu asur bishtiyya:

clarification.explanation: Gentile contact that forbids wine for benefit is when he touches the wine (with his hand, foot, or an object in his hand) intentionally and moves it slightly (a stirring), even a small stirring; or when he drank from the jug; or when he lifted an open vessel with wine and stirred it slightly — all of these forbid for benefit. But if he touched the wine with no stirring at all, this is permitted for benefit, and only forbidden for drinking.
takeaways: Gentile contact forbids for benefit only if there was some stirring (movement of the wine); contact without stirring is forbidden only for drinking, permitted for benefit.

paragraphs: Achaz haggoy bikli patucha veshikshek apillu lo higbihha hakkeli velo naga bayyayin hare zeh asur bahanaa, bammeh debarim amurim? keshehaya hakkeli patucha abal im haya hakkeli satum ben haya male ben haya chaser hare zeh muttar lekulle alema deen derek nissuk bekak vaapillu dehakkeli zekukit shehayyayin nireh mibbachutz shari mippene shehu satum veayyen tiperet adam siman l"g ot b' vaapillu im hakkeli patucha im higbiho haggoy velo shikshek velo naga bayyayin hare zeh muttar bishtiyya vekol shekken deeno oser bingiat hakkeli bilbad shello naga bayyayin velo higbihha velo shikshek devadday shari veim haya haggoy nose keli shebbo hayyayin patucha veyisrael holek acharayv im hu chaser velo shiksheko muttar bishtiyya v"g dei epshar lelek apillu leat beli qetzat ninua mikkol maqom ninua kol dehu la miqqere shikshuk kannizkar bebet yosep veken natal keli sheen bo ella sheyarim yayin "p shemmehallek kedarko shari dedabar muat kazeh eno meqarqesh behilluko. veayyen tiperet adam:

clarification.explanation: If the gentile held an open vessel and stirred it, even without lifting it and without touching the wine directly — this is already forbidden for benefit. But this law is true only when the vessel is open; if the vessel is sealed (closed), whether full or partly empty, it is entirely permitted according to all opinions, since there is no manner of libation when the vessel is closed — even a glass vessel through which the wine is visible (but which is sealed) is permitted. Even if the vessel is open, if the gentile only lifted it without stirring and without touching the wine directly, it is permitted even for drinking. And all the more so, mere contact with the vessel itself (without touching the wine, without lifting, without stirring) is certainly permitted. If a gentile carried an open vessel with wine and a Jew walked behind him, and the vessel had a small amount of wine (partly empty) which he did not stir, this is permitted for drinking — since slight movement alone from ordinary walking is not considered stirring.
takeaways: A gentile merely holding and stirring an open vessel (without even touching the wine itself) forbids it for benefit; but a sealed vessel, or an open vessel merely lifted without stirring, is permitted.
Ordinary walking with a vessel (without deliberate stirring) is not considered forbidding stirring.

paragraphs: Nitareb setam yenam shel akku"m o yayin kasher shennaga bo haakku"m hare zeh asur bishtiyya apillu bekol shehu veen lo bittul beshishshim lehattiro bishtiyya ketzad yaaseh? yimkor et hayyayin kullo laggoy veyiqqach deme yayin haasur shebbo veyashlik leyam hammelach veyehaneh bishar hammaot shel deme yayin hakkasher abal im haya yen nesek gamur asur hakkol bahanaa veim nitareb setam yenam shel yishmeelim o yen maggaam bayyayin hakkasher hare zeh batel beshishshim umuttar kol hayyayin bishtiyya:

clarification.explanation: If gentiles' ordinary wine (or kosher wine touched by a gentile) became mixed in any quantity with other wine, it forbids it for drinking with no possibility of nullification in sixty. The solution: sell all the wine to a gentile, take the monetary payment representing the forbidden wine's portion and throw it into the Dead Sea (or a similar place where no one will benefit from it), and use the rest of the money (representing the kosher wine's portion). But if this concerns actual libation wine (poured for idolatry), the entire mixture is forbidden even for benefit and cannot be sold at all. By contrast, if Ishmaelites' ordinary wine, or wine touched by Ishmaelites, mixed into kosher wine, it is nullified in sixty and everything is permitted for drinking.
takeaways: A mixture of gentiles' ordinary wine with kosher wine is forbidden for drinking without nullification in sixty; the solution is selling to a gentile and discarding the value of the forbidden portion.
A mixture of Ishmaelites' wine (or their contact) with kosher wine is nullified in sixty and permitted for drinking.

paragraphs: Akku"m shennaga beyayin shel yisrael lehakis kede leasero alayv ulehapsido hare zeh muttar dibhay gavna lo gazeru rabbanan vaapillu deen yodeim ken ella raq beumdanut hammokichot veayyen "bet yosep" siman ql"b v"keneset haggedola" sham behaggahat habbet yosep ot va"v veayyen mvr"m behaggahat hashshulchan. vedarke mosheh sop siman qk"d. mihu haramba"m za"l oser uleinyan halaka behepsed merubbeh vadday yesh lehattir vaapillu behepsed muat hammaqqel lo hipsid, mihu baal nepesh yachmir leatzmo vetabo alayv beraka:

clarification.explanation: A gentile who touched a Jew's wine with intent to anger and harm him (not to drink it) — the wine is permitted, since the Sages did not decree the gentile-contact prohibition in such a case. This is true even when it is not known with certainty that the intent was to anger, but only by assessment (estimation) proving this. The Rambam disagrees and forbids in this case. The practical halacha: in a case of great loss, one should certainly permit it; and even in a case of minor loss, the lenient view has not lost out; but one who wishes to be stringent with himself is blessed.
takeaways: A gentile who touched a Jew's wine to anger him (not to drink) — the wine is permitted, even if known only by assessment; in great loss, certainly permitted, and even in minor loss the lenient view stands, though stringency is blessed.

paragraphs: Chometz gamur lav bar nissuk hu vekol shemmashlikin oto al haaretz vehu mebabea babua gamur vechazaq shemmaaleh reticha zo achar zo baqqarqa lo qasheh velo rapeh hare zeh chometz gamur veeno neesar bemagga goy, abal im eno chazaq kak neesar bemagga goy mishshum deen anachnu beqiin bazeh veshemma adayin hu yayin veayyen keneset haggedola haggahat habbet yosep ot n' yeuyyan sham veyayin mazug kol zeman sheyyesh bo taam yayin asur bemagga haggoy. ume boser shehu anabim shello nitbashshelu "p sheadayin hem chamutzim harbeh hammayim hayyotzeim mehem niqraim yayin veneesarim bemagga goy lepi sheen anachnu beqiin ad matay niqra boser, mihu me boser shennetanam bemaakol shennitshattena tamam veenam neesarim bemagga vekol shekken heka debishshelam betabshil deshare bevadday:

clarification.explanation: Full-fledged vinegar is not included in libation (there is no manner of pouring vinegar for idolatry), and is therefore not forbidden by gentile contact — but only if it is truly full vinegar, that is, when poured on the ground it bubbles strongly and continuously. If the bubbling is weaker, the vinegar is forbidden by gentile contact, since we have no reliable way to know if it is truly full vinegar or still wine. Diluted wine (mixed with water) that still has a wine taste is forbidden by gentile contact. Unripe-grape juice (very sour juice from unripe grapes) is still considered wine and forbidden by gentile contact, since we have no reliable way to determine exactly when grapes are considered unripe. But if the unripe juice was placed into a food that changed its taste, it is not forbidden by contact — and all the more so if it was cooked in a dish, which is certainly permitted.
takeaways: Full vinegar (with strong bubbling) is not forbidden by gentile contact; weak vinegar, diluted wine, and unripe-grape juice are forbidden by contact, out of concern they are still considered wine.
Unripe-grape juice mixed into food that changed its taste (or cooked in a dish) is not forbidden.

paragraphs: Mumar oser hayyayin bemaggao veim hu mumar akku"m oser gam bahanaa kepi haumma sheddabaq bah veim hu mumar yishmeeli oser bishtiyya bilbad. vaabadim ushepachot shel yisrael shello malu velo nitgayyeru oserin hayyayin bemaggaan:

clarification.explanation: An apostate Jew (who converted to another religion) forbids wine by his contact, and if he apostatized to idolatry — forbids it even for benefit, following the law of the nation he joined. If he apostatized to the Ishmaelite religion — forbids only for drinking. Male and female slaves of a Jew who were not circumcised and did not convert — their contact also forbids the wine.
takeaways: An apostate Jew forbids wine by contact following the law of the nation he joined (idolatry — even for benefit; Ishmaelites — only for drinking); uncircumcised, unconverted slaves' contact likewise forbids it.

paragraphs: Katab midrash talpiyyot beshem rabbenu menachem habbabli za"l deim haggoy raa et hayyayin "p shello naga bo yesh lehachmir shello lishtoto veken katebu beshem hashshela"h za"l, abal middina muttar bevadday im haggoy hazzeh eno akku"m ella hu middat yishmael apillu chumera umiddat chasidut lekka bazeh:

clarification.explanation: According to Midrash Talpiot, citing Rabbi Menachem HaBavli, if a gentile only looked at the wine without touching it at all, one should be stringent and not drink it (so was also written in the name of the Shelah). But by strict law, this is entirely permitted, certainly if this gentile does not worship idols but follows the Ishmaelite religion — in which case there is not even a stringency or measure of piety involved.
takeaways: A gentile merely looking at wine (without contact) — some are stringent, but by strict law it is permitted, and with an Ishmaelite there is not even a proper stringency involved.

paragraphs: En mapqidin velo sholechin yayin beyad haggoy ella im ken hu chatum bishte chotamot veim satam haqqanqan bistima mehuddeqet yapa bechozeq kederek shessotemin haqqanqan bishbil shello yazub hayyayin mimmennu hare zeh nechshab chotam echad veim qashar alayv qesher meshunneh hare zeh chotam sheni vekol zeh hu lepi daat harab abodat haggereshunni vaperach matteh aharon abal harab chiqre leb yoreh dea cheleq ' siman r" piqpeq bazeh usebira lah dela mehanne zeh ella bemapqid beyad haggoy abal im sholeach beyad haggoy meir lair en setima hamhuddeqet nechshebet lechotam echad ella yaaseh kak yistom hakkeli bipqaq mehuddaq veaach"k yaticha al hassetima zepet sheqqorin bearbe ly"k vehave zeh chotam echad ukemo shekkatab bedap rp" ammud g veal zeh hly"k yachtom bechotam shello o yiqshor alayv qesher meshunneh ubazeh naasu b' chotamot veim lo asa ticha shel zepet hannizkar, ella qesher al piv shel hakkeli shene mine qesharim shekkol echad hu qesher meshunneh bipne atzmo veenam shavim zeh im zeh chashib shette chotamot veshari veim katab alayv biktibat yado shette otiyyot have kishte chotamot abal tzarik sheyyakkir chabero ketibat yado velav davqa hayyayin bae shette chotamot ella kol sheyyesh bo issur min hattora tzarik shette chotamot abal im issuro middibre soperim day lo bechotam echad:

clarification.explanation: Wine should not be deposited with or sent by a gentile unless it is sealed with two seals (so the gentile cannot open and touch it without it being noticed). Sealing a jug tightly in the ordinary manner (so the wine does not leak) is considered one seal; tying an additional, unusual knot beyond that is considered a second seal. There is a dispute among the authorities: according to one view, this suffices for mere deposit, but if the wine is sent by a gentile from city to city, something stronger is needed: sealing the vessel with a tight stopper, then smearing tar over the seal (one seal), and stamping the tar with a personal seal or an unusual knot (a second seal). Alternatively, one may tie two different kinds of knots on the vessel's mouth, each distinct from the other — this too counts as two seals. And if one wrote two letters on the vessel in his own handwriting (which his friend recognizes), this too counts as two seals. The requirement of two seals is not limited to wine — anything whose prohibition is Torah-level requires two seals, and only a rabbinic-level prohibition suffices with one seal.
takeaways: Sending wine by a gentile requires two independent seals (such as a tight seal plus an unusual knot, or two letters in recognized handwriting) — so he cannot touch it without it being noticed.
The requirement of two seals applies to any Torah-level prohibition, not only wine; a rabbinic prohibition suffices with one seal.
